title: Uddhava Arrives in Vrindavan
subtitle: Nanda longs for Krishna as Yashoda weeps
story:
Uddhava reached Nanda's Vraja as the sun went down.

The village at dusk was a thing alive. Powerful bulls, scenting the cows, bellowed and fought in the lanes; white calves leaped this way and that, so that the whole settlement seemed dressed in them; and the women sang as they worked, singing the auspicious deeds of Bala and Krishna, the two brothers the village had raised and lost. Every home bore the marks of worship — the fire, the sun, the guest, the cow, the Brahmana, the ancestors, the gods, each honored in its turn — and around the settlement the forests stood in full flower, loud with the calling of birds.

Uddhava walked through the lanes slowly, taking it all in — the smoke of the evening fires, the lowing of the cows coming home, the songs rising and falling. So this was the world Krishna spoke of in his quiet moments; no wonder his heart had never quite left it.

When Nanda learned who had come, he hurried out to meet him: Krishna's own companion, his beloved attendant, a traveler from the city that had taken his son. He embraced Uddhava and honored him as he would have honored Vasudeva himself, and pressed upon him the finest food the house could offer, and seated him comfortably on a couch. Only then, with his guest at rest, did the old man's questions begin to spill out.

Is our friend well, he asked — the son of Shura, our Krishna? By good fortune, he said, the sinner Kamsa had been killed, with all his followers, by the very evil he had done. But does Krishna remember us? Does he remember his mother, his friends, his playmates? Will Govinda ever come back, even once, to look upon his own people?

Before Uddhava could answer, Nanda was already answering himself, the memories crowding in. He remembered how Krishna had sheltered them from the forest fire, and from wind and rain, from the great bull and from the serpent. He remembered his heroic deeds, and the playful sidelong glance of him. He remembered the rivers, the mountains, the forests — every one of them adorned by the touch of Krishna's feet. The more he remembered, the more he wondered: surely Krishna and Rama were the best of the gods, come down to walk among men. Who else could have broken the great bow, tall as three palm trees, as an elephant king snaps a staff? Who else could have brought down Kamsa, strong as ten thousand elephants, together with the two wrestlers and the royal elephant? And the demons of Krishna's boyhood — Pralamba, Dhenuka, Arishta, Trinavarta, Baka — one after another they had fallen to the two brothers in the very fields where Nanda's cattle still grazed.

And as Nanda spoke, Yashoda listened — and wept. She had held herself steady while the messenger spoke of Mathura; it was the boyhood deeds that undid her, the demon fights in the pastures and the fire in the forest, because those were the years when he had still been hers to hold.

So the evening passed in Nanda's house: the honored guest upon the couch, the old cowherd recounting wonders, and the mother of Krishna weeping quietly at the sound of her son's name.
reflection: Nanda's questions run straight to the only thing that matters to him: not what Krishna has conquered, but whether Krishna remembers — his mother, his friends, his playmates. The village keeps Krishna alive by singing his deeds, and the measure of its love is remembrance.
next_story_tease: Only then did Uddhava find the words to speak the message Krishna had entrusted to him.
hero_scene: At dusk in Vrindavan, the aged Nanda embraces Uddhava at the threshold of his house, while behind them Yashoda weeps at the sound of her son's name and the village glows with lamps as bulls low and women sing the deeds of Bala and Krishna.
